This is what the mysterious Denisovans looked like

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Artist depiction of the heavy set facial features of a Denisovan.Credit: Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology/Chinese Academy of Sciences

A low, sloping forehead, a massive brow ridge that curves backwards, rectangle-like eye sockets, flat cheeks and a moderately elevated bridge of the nose. Taken together, these features are the hallmarks of the ancient humans called the Denisovans, say researchers who studied a trove of fossilized skull fragments, teeth and jaws found in northern China.

“We are finally starting to put a face to the Denisovan,” says Sally Wasef, a palaeogeneticist at the Queensland University of Technology in Brisbane, Australia.

Denisovans were first described in 2010, after researchers sequenced genetic material from a mysterious finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia and found that it did not resemble that of Homo sapiens or Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis). Ancient proteins have since been used to identify remains from other parts of Asia as Denisovan, including the first near-complete Denisovan skull found near Harbin, which helped to put a face on the ancient humans.

Researchers report in Nature1 today that they have an even better idea of what Denisovans looked like after analysing the physical features of remains that belong to a collection of 20 fossils found in Xujiayao.

The Xujiayao remains are at least 130,000 years old and were found in the 1970s, alongside animal remains and tools. At the time, it was unclear what type of human these fossils belonged to, and they were classified as a species called Homo juluensis. By analysing ancient proteins from some of the fossils, Qiaomei Fu, a geneticist at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing, and her team identified the remains as Denisovan.

Wasef says that ancient-protein analysis is a valuable tool to complement DNA studies, particularly because proteins can survive longer than can DNA without fully degrading. Although DNA provides more-detailed information about an individual, protein analysis can still yield useful information about who an individual is related to.

Fabrice Demeter, a palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen, says that the findings add to growing evidence that Denisovans were a widespread and potentially diverse group of humans. “The study represents a major step forward” in our understanding of what these humans could have looked like and where they lived.

Fu’s team analysed small fragments of proteins, called peptides, from two Xujiayao bones and compared them with peptides found in humans and Neanderthals. They found a single amino-acid change that was present in multiple peptides from the Xujiayao bones and other East Asian fossils and is a known genetic marker for identifying Denisovans. The amino-acid change was not seen in human or Neanderthal samples.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03360-0

Clarification 21 October 2026: A previous version of this story used the word skulls instead of skull fragments.

The Bursar

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). Marissa Lingen has published more than 100 short stories in venues such as Analog, Lightspeed and Tor.com.

The Bursar shook Cerise’s hand with firm confidence. “We don’t expect you to be familiar with procedures,” he said. “Orientation for our new parents is standard. Don’t be embarrassed to ask questions.”

“I suppose when Lorelei is my age the parents will take it for granted.” Cerise smiled in self-deprecation.

The Bursar nodded. “Of course, we expect our system to progress a great deal more by then. Now, your daughter Lorelei — she’s five?”

“Five in June,” Cerise agreed. “A normal, happy little girl, we’d like to think.”

“Our programme will help keep her that way.” The Bursar gestured for Cerise to follow him. The halls were bright and spacious, decorated with printouts of student artwork.

“Lorelei will have her own cubicle, kindergarten through graduation,” said the Bursar, gesturing at one of the dim nooks off the bright hallway. “One advantage of our programme is decreased contagion — although that’s not its main appeal.”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Cerise peered in at the tiny, still form. She felt like a voyeur into this strange industrial transformation of sleep. She forced a laugh. “A far cry from showing me the gym and the art room, isn’t it?”

The Bursar pursed his lips. “Our students do experience those things. In some ways the virtual environment is superior — you and I didn’t see a new gymnasium remodel more than once, if ever. Lorelei will never experience anything but. No matter how the state of the art changes, our experience changes with it.”

They finished the tour in silence — not much to see except for the nurse’s office, which didn’t look much like the nurses’ offices of Cerise’s childhood except for its antiseptic gleam. Satisfied, the Bursar escorted her back to his office.

“We used to think that children just had to take whatever life threw at them,” he beamed, relaxing into his leather chair and leaving Cerise to perch on a wooden one. “What a terrible idea, raising children on random trauma! Then we reversed course and over-restricted them until their prefrontal cortexes developed.” He shook his head. “Lunacy. Learning requires error.”

“Of course,” said Cerise stiffly, one of that protected cohort herself.

But the Bursar was giving his favourite speech and could not be distracted. “Our calibrated experience will allow Lorelei to only experience the proper amount of error, conflict and pain. We can’t do what some of the upper-end models do, but at your budget … I think you’ll be pleased with her educational experience.”

“What about external … problems? Obviously we try not to have any,” Cerise hurried to explain. “But what if Lorelei has a grandparent with cancer, or something traumatic like that?”

“It’s crucial for you to report to us regularly. Even small trauma — she twists her ankle playing at the park — is used to customize her programme. We’d substitute a nurturing experience in for a challenge there. We’ll assess her reactions constantly, fitting her challenges to her means of addressing them, but our weekly report from parents is crucial. Just think what would happen if we were giving her scenarios like fighting with a friend at recess on top of her parents getting a divorce! Disaster.”

“We’re not getting a divorce,” Cerise blurted defensively, and then made herself add, “I know, you just meant … for example. But to take your example, can she really have fights with friends at recess? Do you connect the children’s simulations to each other?”

“Absolutely not!” snapped the Bursar. “Children are chaotic! You might as well send her to traditional school if that was all you cared for her brain development.”

“But … doesn’t that mean she won’t share childhood memories with anybody?” Cerise thought about the time Lucy Meisner threw up on a field trip to the zoo, the time she and Tony Azar got in trouble for hiding at the end of recess and how it made them laugh decades later.

“Many adults don’t remain close with their classmates from traditional schooling, either,” said the Bursar stiffly. “We feel the trade-off is well worth it.”

“I understand.” Cerise sighed. “So I expect you’ll have the fee structure to go over.”

His face closed disapprovingly. “I will direct you to that department on your way out.”

Huge mapping study reveals how your brain tracks what your body is feeling

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

The region called the insula is buried deep beneath the brain’s wrinkled surface (artist’s illustration).Credit: Alexander Leemans/UMC Utrecht/Science Photo Library

The region called the insula is buried deep beneath the brain’s wrinkled surface (artist’s illustration).Credit: Alexander Leemans/UMC Utrecht/Science Photo Library

Scientists have mapped one of the most mysterious parts of the human brain in unprecedented detail1. Their results show how this region, the insular cortex or insula, is organized to support the brain’s processing of bodily sensations such as pain. The mapping also details a pathway that allows the cortex — the seat of higher-order cognition — to work with the insula to affect bodily perceptions.

One region of the insula is responsible for the feeling of pain in certain parts of the body. Another region generates sensations, such as nausea, felt by the internal organs. A third region, at the front of the insula, ‘talks’ to other brain areas involved in cognition and emotion, suggesting that it influences not only sensations, but also how the brain interprets them.

Contrary to previous thinking, the insula is “not just reading the body. It is partly influencing the story about how the body should be felt,” says study co-author Josef Parvizi, a physician-scientist at Stanford University in California.

The study is “quite a feat”, says Lucina Uddin, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. It’s also one of the most comprehensive studies on the insula and how it produces bodily sensations, she adds.

The findings were published today in Nature.

The insula has been notoriously difficult to study in detail because it’s located deep in the brain. Previous studies have suggested that this hard-to-reach region is involved in receiving signals — such as pain or pressure — from various parts of the body, then processing them into sensations that we experience. But most research on the human insula has relied on brain-imaging techniques to capture what happens in the insula when various sensations arise, Parvizi says.

To build a more detailed picture, Parvizi and his colleagues needed to find a way to send electrical signals to various parts of the insula in people and assess the bodily sensations that occur as a result. But implanting electrodes deep in the brains of healthy people would be unethical. So, the researchers turned to 87 people who’d had electrodes implanted in their brains for medical reasons.

The brain’s map of the body is surprisingly stable — even after a limb is lost

The brain’s map of the body is surprisingly stable — even after a limb is lost

In experiments that spanned more than a decade, Parvizi and his colleagues sent electrical currents through the electrodes into a variety of sites in the participants’ insulas.

Stimulating the rear of the insula produced pain, heat and other sensations — including tingling and numbness — in specific areas of the participants’ bodies, such as the arm or leg. Meanwhile, participants experienced more ‘visceral’ sensations, including nausea, pressure and feelings of fullness in their chest, when the researchers sent electrical currents to the middle of the insula.

Global greenhouse-gas emissions were roughly flat from 2024 to 2025.Credit: Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty

Despite a possible plateau in global greenhouse-gas emissions last year, average temperatures are set to hurtle past 2 °C of warming around the middle of the century, barring a major acceleration in emissions cuts, finds the United Nations’ latest report on climate change.

The super El Niño is already wreaking havoc: here’s what’s in store

The super El Niño is already wreaking havoc: here’s what’s in store

“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 °C limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” said outgoing UN secretary-general António Guterres in a press briefing announcing the report — an annual accounting of progress towards tackling climate change published by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) on 21 October. Guterres pointed to the extended heatwaves, massive wildfires and deadly floods that have disrupted much of the world in 2026. He called for faster action from governments to cut emissions by transitioning away from fossil fuels, expanding clean electricity and reversing deforestation.

Under current policies, scientists estimate warming to peak at 2.6 °C to 2.8 °C above pre-industrial levels this century — substantially exceeding the 2 °C upper limit of the 2015 Paris Agreement targets to avoid the most dangerous consequences of climate change. There is also a smaller, 10% chance of warming exceeding 3.4 °C on the current trajectory, which researchers say would be catastrophic. Even under a scenario in which countries achieve all existing emissions pledges, the report projects 2.1 °C of warming.

Although the 1.5 °C goal to limit the worst effects climate change is out of reach — 2026 is projected to be the second year in which temperatures have surpassed that level of warming — the report maintains that it might be possible to ‘overshoot’ that target, then bring temperatures back down through rapid decarbonization and a massive expansion of carbon dioxide removal.

UNEP’s assessment comes ahead of November’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, at which governments will take stock of efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change. “The emissions gap is now a leadership gap. And the world is running out of time and excuses to close it,” Guterres said.

There is some good news in this year’s report. Initial estimates show that global greenhouse-gas emissions in 2025 were about the same or slightly lower than in 2024. That was mainly due to a decrease in emissions from land-use activities, particularly as a result of a quiet year for wildfires after unprecedented blazes in 2024.

That would be the first decline seen since the COVID-19 pandemic, and it could represent the start of a plateau or even a peak in emissions (see ‘Have emissions peaked?’). But researchers caution that a single year is not enough to determine if this is a lasting shift.

Source: United Nations Environment Programme

“Global emissions will have to fall several per cent before there can be any certainty that they have peaked,” says Lauri Myllyvirta, a researcher at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a research organization in Helsinki. “Until then, one particularly hot summer or other cyclical development can cause a jump above the preceding peak, even if the structural trend is downward.”

Another encouraging trend is the rapid expansion of renewable sources of energy. Clean-energy capacity has increased around three times faster than was anticipated since 2015, and solar energy has expanded seven times faster than expected as costs of solar panelshave fallen.

Myllyvirta points out that even if this year doesn’t represent an emissions peak, the report projects a 5–8% drop by 2030 relative to 2025 levels. “The door to a much larger reduction than this over the next five years is open,” he says, as clean energy accelerates, fossil fuels become costlier, and because of the potential for China and India to overachieve their promised emissions cuts.

UN finally admits global warming will shoot past 1.5 ºC climate limit

Emma Pierson is at the University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, California 94703, USA.

Although people report increasing trepidation about the effects of artificial intelligence across many domains, health care emerges as a rare area of some optimism1. AI tools, in the form of large language models (LLMs), such as the chatbot ChatGPT, are widely used for health advice. It is estimated that one-third of US adults turn to chatbots for answers to health questions2, and globally it has been suggested that about 230 million people ask ChatGPT health and wellness questions every week3. Writing in Nature, Heydari et al.4 present their response to this enormous demand by creating and assessing an AI personal health ‘agent’, which is designed to analyse an individual’s health data and offer advice.

To heal sick cities, scientists and residents must work together

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sarah Wild is a freelance journalist in Canterbury, UK.

Tollulah Oni, right, running with teammates during an event at the International Conference on Sustainable Urban Mobility in Lagos, Nigeria, in 2025.Credit: LAMATA/The 2025 International Conference on Sustainable Urban Mobility Run

In 2016, public-health physician Tolullah Oni was jogging through the streets of Dakar when she saw someone doing push-ups in the middle of a busy roundabout. Cars were puffing fumes around him as the Sun baked down. As a physician, she knew that this had health implications.

More than half of the global population now lives in urban areas, but many cities are not conducive to human health and well-being. Oni, who is a researcher at University of Cambridge, UK, describes herself as an urban epidemiologist whose patients are cities. She works with colleagues around the world to diagnose and treat ‘sick’ cities with the goal of improving the health and quality of life of their inhabitants. This involves monitoring several variables, such as air quality and temperature, and their impact on the city’s residents. Those data can inform advocacy and interventions.

How I harness research to inform humanitarian relief efforts

How I harness research to inform humanitarian relief efforts

Frustrated by a lack of infrastructure on the ground in such cities, and by the struggle to connect researchers and residents, she set up the non-profit organization UrbanBetter in 2019 to support her research and advocacy. By providing training on data collection and analysis, the organization helps citizens and local researchers to diagnose their own cities and to use that evidence to lobby for change. Its research arm, the UrbanBetter Academy, has a centre in Cambridge, and its civic arm, called Cityzens Hubs, operates in 11 cities in Africa, as well as in Bogotá and Bangkok.

Oni, who was born in Nigeria, identifies as African diaspora, which she classifies as a “sixth distinct region of the African continent”. Now based in the United Kingdom, she recognizes the friction that comes with trying to treat cities that she does not live in. Oni tells Nature how she wants to create lasting virtual infrastructure through UrbanBetter that channels the diaspora’s intellectual capital back into the continent and heals sick cities.

Cities can’t tell you that they’re sick, so you must bring the symptoms to light first. What are the lungs or air quality doing? What is happening in the green spaces? How is the city metabolizing energy? What is happening to its waste? If you don’t have the data, you don’t know whether the city is sick and in a lot of our cities, we’re not even measuring those things.

It is important that the people who are identifying the symptoms are on the ground in that city, rather than me, a professor, sitting thousands of kilometres away in Cambridge. People there are breathing the air and moving through the city. We have to equip local people with the skill set to diagnose a city. The diagnostic tests can be done by sensors and their data can be mapped.

In cities, we need treatments to be grounded in lived realities. Outsiders can assess a city and propose a solution, backed by evidence, but it might not work for many reasons. We need to include residents. They can identify priority areas and advocate for change. For example, in Nairobi, a group of Cityzens collected air-pollution data and convened their own community assembly in 2025 to identify potential solutions, such as cleaner public transport, adding trees and green spaces and reducing open burning of rubbish. These points fed directly into the government’s Nairobi City County Air Quality Action Plan.

Developing treatments for a city is a collective effort and accountability is spoon-feeding that medicine in the form of small, incremental changes so that the city can get better.

I set up UrbanBetter in 2019 as an experimental platform that would situate research differently by combining it with action and advocacy. We started with a US$300,000 unrestricted grant from the funding organization Unorthodox Philanthropy, which is sponsored by the Lampert Byrd Foundation based in San Francisco, California.

Each of UrbanBetter’s hubs has different strengths — Lagos works on physical activity, air pollution and heat, whereas Bogotá has done work on transport, cycling and car-free days. This means that when another city wants to work in a new area, they don’t have to reinvent the wheel.

Ahead of the 2025 Lagos City Marathon, the local Cityzens Hub partnered with World Athletics’ project Running for Clean Air. The marathon takes place in February, which is among the hottest times of year in Lagos, and the city has high levels of air pollution.

I paused my PhD for 11 years to help save Madagascar’s seas

I paused my PhD for 11 years to help save Madagascar’s seas

Throughout 2025, a group of residents ran the marathon route each month, starting in the January before the marathon. They wore air-quality sensors and collected geotagged data with the UrbanBetter app. Some runners found that there was a 60% reduction in air pollution on the actual marathon day because cars were barred from the roads. These findings have informed a shift in transportation-policy implementation in the city, which is now targeting net-zero emissions by 2050. Government initiatives include increased cycling and walking, an overhaul of public transport and increased air-quality monitoring.

The Cityzens Hub then identified heat as another major issue for city dwellers, so they reached out to the UrbanBetter Academy for help analysing complex data. In 2025, researchers from UrbanBetter, local partner institutions and the Lagos Transport Authority received a £2-million [roughly US$2.6-million] grant from the biomedical funding charity Wellcome to investigate heat exposure and health risks in Lagos in a project called Hotsteppers. This is how UrbanBetter works — that research question about heat came from people on the ground raising the issue.

Most white dwarf stars are white, but analysis now shows that a few come in a rainbow of colours — even green, which has never before been spotted in a star.

<i>De novo</i> design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1–5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6–8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage’s polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4–6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.

It details the fabrication and measurement of single-molecule Au-helicene-Au junctions and presents experimental analyses of their operation as molecular machines, together with control experiments and a discussion of alternative explanations for the observed effects. It also includes density functional theory calculations of the molecular junction structure and rotational potential landscape, as well as quantum electronic transport calculations. Finally, it presents a microscopic theoretical framework that explains the current-induced torque, molecular rotation, and current enhancement underlying the observed behaviour.

Daily briefing: The tell-tale features of a Denisovan

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Artist depiction of the heavy set facial features of a Denisovan.Credit: Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology/Chinese Academy of Sciences

A low, sloping forehead, a massive brow ridge, rectangle-like eye sockets, flat cheeks, and a moderately elevated bridge of the nose were probably the hallmark features of Denisovans — a mysterious ancient-human species. Using fossilized skull fragments, teeth and jaws, researchers identified some visual features that would have set Denisovans apart from other early-human species, such as the flattened, elongated skull shape. A knowledge of these unique features could help researchers classify other fossils that couldn’t previously be identified as Denisovan.

The emergence of mental-health conditions in teenagers could be forecast by the speed at which certain regions of their brain develop. A study of nearly 12,000 young people in the United States suggests that vulnerability to conditions such as depression in adolescents could involve disruption of the brain’s developmental timeline and could be set in motion by genes that are active before birth. The findings reveal small population-level patterns, says systems neuroscientist Avram Holmes, but can’t be used to track the trajectory of an individual child.

Reference: bioRxiv preprint (not peer reviewed)

A new analysis of ancient artifacts suggests that a woman named Meretneith, who was buried in a lavish tomb around 5,000 years ago, might have been Egypt’s first female ruler. Egyptologists Sue Kelly and Crystal Miller analysed digitally enhanced photographs of serekhs — hieroglyphs that indicate a person ruled at the time of their death — that named the king Djer, and possibly Meretneith, that were found on objects in a separate tomb. They found that one features the goddess Neith, "a symbol no male ruler ever used”, Kelly says, which hints that Meretneith held true royal authority, not that of a consort or regent.

Reference: Prague Egyptological Studies paper

Scientists have mapped the mysterious insula in the human brain in unprecedented detail. The results detail how this region is organized to support the brain’s processing of bodily sensation: one region is responsible for the feeling of pain in some body parts, a second generates sensations such as nausea felt by internal organs and a third ‘talks’ to other brain areas involved in emotion and cognition. The latter area allows for the insula to work with the cortex — the seat of higher-order cognition — to affect how the brain interprets various sensations.

A phase II/III trial of a vaccine against Ebola could see its first doses administered as soon as this week in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where there have been more than 9,500 known cases and more than 4,600 deaths, reports Science. The trial, named Tumaini — Swahili for “hope” — will first use a vaccine called Ervebo that targets a ‘mismatched’ ebolavirus species, ‘Zaire’ — the outbreak in DRC involves the Bundibugyo species. The goal is to add vaccine candidates developed specifically to target Bundibugyo — such as ChAdOx1, developed by a University of Oxford group in the United Kingdom — after they graduate from phase I clinical trials.

Science | 8 min read & Nature | 7 min read (from July)

Robert (Bob) Williamson was a geneticist who dedicated his career to the identification of disease-linked genes and the diagnosis and treatment of single-gene disorders, such as cystic fibrosis (CF) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). “He had almost limitless energy and was an inspiring and generous leader,” writes geneticist Kay Davies, who worked alongside Williamson to narrow down the location of the gene responsible for DMD. Williamson then applied this approach to locate the gene that causes CF, and was an early proponent of gene therapy. He has died, aged 88.

“Making climate change visible is only the first step” for a great graphic, argues digital communications researcher Monika Frątczak. Alongside whether a graph or chart is accurate, “we should also ask who is represented, who is missing and whose experience the data allows us to see”, she writes. By tapping into people’s connection to their own land and community, visualizations can inspire deeper engagement — and an emotional response that can lead to real action.

The timings of traffic lights at busy junctions are often decided by algorithms on the basis of the number of vehicles on the road. But who to prioritize isn’t a purely technical decision, and should instead be debated as a matter of public interest, argues computer scientist Xiaowen Tao (陶晓文). (Nature Cities | 5 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03438-9

Today I’ve learned that despite the name, not all white dwarves are white. Physicists found that a handful of these ultra-dense celestial objects can shine in shades of pink, cyan and even green — a colour never spotted before in stars.

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Terence Tao is a mathematician at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Advanced artificial-intelligence models are transforming mathematics at an astonishing speed. In the past few months, AI-aided proofs — logical arguments that demonstrate why a mathematical result is correct — have been released for hundreds of long-standing maths problems.

Mathematicians might need several months to fully understand the underlying arguments and implications of these automatically derived solutions. As a mathematician who uses AI tools for my own research, I can see that the field has fundamentally transformed. We now urgently need to establish a ‘Maths 2.0’ era, in which ‘proof scarcity’ is no longer a defining feature of the field.

How AI is reshaping discovery in maths and physics

How AI is reshaping discovery in maths and physics

The challenges associated with this new way of doing maths are already evident. Many AI-generated results are not described clearly enough to meet quality standards for publication. Some researchers using AI tools simply move on to the next problem once they have a minimally presentable proof, leaving results that can be difficult for other mathematicians to assess. And it still remains unclear how extensively AI models are drawing on the previous work of mathematicians without providing proper attribution.

The centuries-old practice of openly sharing maths problems is under serious threat because mathematicians are increasingly fearful that disclosing their research directions will lead to their work being ‘scooped’ by a rival who is equipped with a frontier AI model. Graduate students and junior mathematicians used to develop their skills and gain early recognition from their peers by solving such problems. On 6 October, technology firm OpenAI dumped hundreds of solutions to such problems online in one go. It disrupted countless research programmes overnight.

Perhaps the most counter-intuitive consequence is that human understanding of mathematics is falling behind, because AI systems generate results faster than mathematicians can digest and absorb them. Confined to pure mathematics, this ‘proof indigestion’ might be a minor concern. But AI-generated mathematical models deployed in the real world without a matching understanding of their mechanisms could have serious consequences. For example, complex AI-generated models are already used to some extent to determine who qualifies for a bank loan and to measure financial risk in markets. If the complexity of these models outpaces the capacity for humans to understand when they might malfunction, the risks of unforeseen mistakes will grow, affecting the general public.

‘It is incredible’: How AI is transforming mathematics

‘It is incredible’: How AI is transforming mathematics

These negative impacts are not inevitable. Used creatively, and with the right incentives, AI tools could enhance human understanding. It is still possible to change course, through a radical reassessment of the conventional incentive structure of mathematics and by introducing more-responsible practices around AI use.

Teen depression and anxiety predicted by childhood brain development

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Researchers used tens of thousands of magnetic-resonance-imaging scans to map how the brain’s outer layer matures during adolescence.Credit: Zephyr/Science Photo Library

The speed at which regions of the brain mature during early adolescence can forecast the emergence of mental-health conditions up to four years before symptoms develop, according to a study of nearly 12,000 young people in the United States.

Do smartphones and social media really harm teens’ mental health?

Do smartphones and social media really harm teens’ mental health?

By tracking the brains of adolescents over six years in nearly 30,000 scans, researchers mapped how the brain’s outer layer, the cerebral cortex, thins as children grow into teenagers. The team observed that sensory areas of the cortex thinned, or matured, first, followed by the regions responsible for complex thought.

The findings, posted on 11 October on the preprint server bioRxiv1 ahead of peer review, challenge the theory that psychiatric disorders are caused by defects in specific brain circuits. Instead, they indicate that vulnerability to mental-health symptoms could involve disruption of the brain’s developmental timeline and could be set in motion by genes that are active before birth.

The work “provides one of the clearest pictures yet of how the cortex develops from childhood into adolescence”, says Avram Holmes, a systems neuroscientist at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey, who was not involved in the study. “It makes you think about the timing of brain development, not just the location [in the brain], when we look at psychiatric symptoms,” he says.

But he cautions that the population-level patterns found in the study — trends that become visible only when averaging data across large numbers of people — are subtle and cannot yet be used in the clinic to forecast the mental-health trajectory of an individual child.

During childhood and adolescence, the cerebral cortex thins. Neuroscientists attribute this process to the pruning of unused connections between neurons, which helps the brain to operate efficiently.

Mini models of the human brain are revealing how this complex organ takes shape

Mini models of the human brain are revealing how this complex organ takes shape

Researchers have long suspected that disruptions to cortical thinning contribute to mental illness, because psychiatric conditions such as depression are often diagnosed during late adolescence, when the thinning process is winding down. But proving that link has been difficult because brain-imaging studies have historically relied on small sample sizes or single snapshots in time.

To overcome these hurdles, study co-author Jacqueline Clauss, a child psychiatrist at the University of Iowa in Iowa City, and her colleagues turned to data from a massive project that is tracking nearly 12,000 children from around the age of nine. Participants’ brains are scanned every two years, and their parents complete surveys annually about their children’s mental-health symptoms.

When analysing the data, Clauss and her colleagues found that rather than thinning at a steady rate, brain regions change following a distinct trajectory that fits an S-shaped curve. Thinning of a region of the cortex initially accelerates, then proceeds steadily before decelerating as the region nears maturity.

A first for CRISPR: powerful prime editing alters DNA directly in the human body

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The method called prime editing can make fine-scale edits to DNA (artist’s illustration).Credit: Patrick Landmann/Science Photo Library

A powerful gene-editing technique has been used to edit DNA directly in a person’s body — the first known instance of such a treatment.

The milestone treatment is part of a clinical trial of prime editing, a technique that can alter DNA with more precision than standard CRISPR–Cas9 methods can. In this case, prime editing was used to treat a condition called Wilson’s disease by rewriting DNA in liver cells, to erase a mutation that prevents them from eliminating excess copper.

Prime Medicine, a biotechnology company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, announced that it had treated the first person in its trial earlier this month. It expects to announce the first results from the study next year.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

“I never dreamed that in my lifetime I would see this applied to my rare disease,” says Rhonda Rowland, president of the Wilson Disease Association in Atlanta, Georgia. “It’s going to be a really exciting year.”

In launching the trial, Prime Medicine joins a host of companies aiming to engineer cells directly in the body, rather than using the standard method of extracting a person’s cells, editing their DNA in a laboratory and then reinjecting the altered cells. Rewriting DNA in the body, or in vivo, is appealing because manufacturing and administering the treatment might be much cheaper and faster than making a bespoke therapy for each person from their own cells.

But in vivo approaches have their own challenges, says Krishanu Saha, a biomedical engineer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “It depends on what types of risks you’re willing to accept,” he says.

Wilson’s disease is caused by mutations in a gene called ATP7B, which encodes a protein that transports excess copper out of the liver. If left untreated, the resulting build-up of copper can cause liver and nerve damage, as well as neurological disorders.

People with Wilson’s disease are eager for a one-and-done treatment for their condition, says Rowland, rather than the current, complicated regimen of copper-clearing molecules and other medicines. And gene editing could, in theory, provide a lasting solution by correcting the faulty ATP7B gene.

So far, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved only one gene-editing therapy, called Casgevy, which is used to treat two inherited blood disorders. Casgevy relies on CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing, which is often used to disable genes rather than to rewrite their sequences.

Bizarre CRISPR enzyme kills cancer cells by shredding their DNA

Bizarre CRISPR enzyme kills cancer cells by shredding their DNA

Another form of gene editing, called base editing, can rewrite individual DNA letters, but cannot make the particular corrections needed to fix the most common ATP7B mutations. That left prime editing, a more complex and versatile system that can insert, delete and rewrite segments of DNA. In another clinical trial, Prime Medicine used the technique to treat two people with a rare immune disorder, by rewriting DNA in each participant’s blood stem cells outside of the body and then injecting them back in.

So far, no gene-editing therapies have been approved for use in vivo. But the FDA is expected to issue a decision early next year about an in vivo CRISPR–Cas9 therapy for a condition called hereditary angioedema, which causes severe swelling.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03371-x

I’m expected to work excessive hours in the lab. Should I speak up about my disability?

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A few months ago, I started a PhD at a university in North America. I have a disability that affects both my physical and my mental capacity, and its impact on me fluctuates. The more I can rest, the fewer symptom flare-ups I experience.

Unfortunately, my laboratory has a severe problem with overwork. Most students work 50–60 hours a week and sometimes more. We’re constantly asked to take on new tasks for the projects of our principal investigator (PI), often with tight deadlines. I’ll go into the lab intending to work on my experiments and end up spending all day on my PI’s tasks.

My PI, to whom I have not disclosed my health status, has repeatedly expressed disappointment in my work ethic. I have worked in other labs with different supervisors without facing issues (during my master’s degree, for example), and I know I’m not the only person struggling in this environment: my lab-mates are also burnt out.

Many of my issues are tied to being unable to take breaks while working long hours, often 12–16 hours per day for several days in a row. In previous jobs in which my colleagues and I worked overtime, we could take the equivalent amount of time off either the following week or as holiday time. But in my current lab, we’re expected to come back to work immediately. Sometimes we’re called in on weekends. I can barely keep up because I’m given no time to rest. A task that would take me an hour now takes longer because I’m fighting through pain. When I asked for time off, I received a firm no.

I’m nervous about what I might face in the rest of my programme. I know that I can have the success I want if I find the right environment. I plan to seek accommodations by contacting someone at my university. But should I disclose to my PI? I fear it might make things worse, and that I will face disability stigma. What can I do to make sure myself and other students are well cared for and protected? — A disabled graduate student

“Disability stigma contributes to power imbalances between graduate students and advisers,” says Bonnielin Swenor, director of the Johns Hopkins Disability Health Research Center in Baltimore, Maryland. That stigma is evident from discrepancies in earnings1 and grant outcomes2 between disabled and non-disabled researchers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields, according to her research on US scientists. Understandably, then, “taking action can feel intimidating, and many disabled scientists fear retribution”, she says.

“What you describe is not a personal failure of work ethic,” emphasizes Deepti Sharma, a management researcher at Ahmedabad University in India. You’re in a dysfunctional work environment, in which “your disability made the dysfunction visible to you earlier and more painfully than it did for others”.

Nature’s careers team asked Sharma, Swenor and two other researchers for advice on how disabled graduate students and other people facing similar challenges can protect themselves.

Rebecca Williams, an environmental-law researcher and disability officer at the University of Glasgow, UK, says that there should be staff members who can offer support to students. She recommends investigating what resources are available at your university. These could be from a graduate-student union, a director of graduate studies or university disability services.

In many regions, there is a legal duty not to discriminate against people with disabilities, Williams adds. She also suggests checking whether your university offers any grants or other financial support for the resources that you might need. One source of guidance could be the Job Accommodation Network, a US website providing information on workplace accommodations.

Sharma distinguishes between formal and personal disclosure: “Registering with your university’s disability-services office is a formal, documented process that establishes the accommodations you are entitled to.” At most institutions, the office should inform supervisors only of the accommodations required, not the diagnoses that prompted them. “Personal disclosure to a PI is a separate, discretionary act,” says Sharma, who strongly encourages formal registration as a first step. “Regardless of what you decide about your PI, informal goodwill evaporates under pressure, while documented accommodations do not.”

Williams recommends pausing before deciding whether to approach your PI: “You may want to wait until you have a better sense of your new PI’s supervisory style before you decide how much or little you want to disclose beyond the accommodations that you need.”

To make best use of institutional resources, all four disability advocates stress the importance of documentation. “Keep written records such as e-mails confirming verbal instructions and notes on refused leave requests,” advises Sharma. “Patterns documented over time carry far more weight with a department than any single complaint.” Doing this could also help other students who face similar issues with your PI.

Swenor notes that “keeping detailed records of e-mails and interactions in which disability discrimination occurs is often necessary. As with any form of discrimination, this information provides the needed support if or when you choose to file a complaint or grievance,” she says. “It is also essential to understand your rights and legal protections.”

But, she cautions, keeping a record is only one step. “Formally documenting your needed accommodations does not eliminate bias or discrimination,” she says.

Sharma suggests “building a support structure outside your supervisor’s control: a thesis committee member you trust, a mentor in another department, peers in your cohort”. This support structure could include your head of department or, if it exists, a staff disability network that can connect you to supportive staff members or graduate students who might have relevant lived experience, says Williams.

“Disability in academia is often about finding ‘your people’, who understand what it is to manage health difficulties,” notes Williams, who has written about her own experiences of dealing with chronic illness in academia. “Sometimes finding people that ‘get it’ will help you feel less alone during the process of your PhD, and gauge what a realistic daily or weekly PhD routine might be for you.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02582-6

Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Severe sunburn increases the risk of developing melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer.Credit: Olga Pankova/Getty

A personalized mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of skin cancer returning or the recipient dying by 42% when used alongside an immunotherapy drug, according to long-awaited results for what could become the first approved mRNA vaccine for cancer.

Oncologists regard a risk reduction of 10% as substantial, says Kristen Radford, an immunotherapist at Mater Research in Brisbane. A risk reduction of more than 40% “would send many researchers over the Moon”, adds Seth Cheetham, a geneticist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.

The personalized vaccine, called intismeran, is not designed to prevent skin cancer, or melanoma, from developing in the first place, but to stop it returning in people who have already undergone surgery to remove tumours.

Anticipation for the trial results has been building since August, when the vaccine’s developers — Merck, based in Rahway, New Jersey, and Moderna, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts — announced early positive results. Data from the phase III trial will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on 24 October. But when data were leaked online on 22 October, the companies released the key results.

The stock price for Moderna, a pioneer in mRNA vaccine technology, had been rising since the August announcement, but dropped by around 25% after the leak. Health-care financial analyst Evan Seigerman at BMO Capital Markets in New York City told media company Forbes that such reactions in the stock market probably reflect “inflated expectation into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy”.

The intismeran trial enrolled 1,137 people with moderate to advanced melanoma across 157 centres. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a tailor-made vaccine (intismeran) alongside the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab — which is already used to treat melanoma — or pembrolizumab plus an inactive placebo. Trial leader Georgina Long, an oncologist at Melanoma Institute Australia in Sydney, says participants have so far been followed for around 25 months and will continue to be monitored for several years to determine whether the vaccine improves overall survival. She adds that the therapy did not result in any major harmful side effects.

Roughly 15 years ago, people with advanced melanoma typically survived for only months. Today, nearly 55% are effectively cured with targeted drugs or immunotherapies, says Long. The combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab is designed for people whose cancer could return after surgery and who do not respond to immunotherapy alone, she says.

Jessamy Tiffen, a cancer geneticist at the Centenary Institute in Sydney, says that the trial results are exciting, but that only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years. “Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them,” she says. Furthermore, some people did not respond to the vaccine, she says.

Long says that her team will conduct a statistical analysis to identify who is most likely to benefit from the treatment.

To develop intismeran, Long and her colleagues sequenced DNA from a sample of each participant’s tumour to identify mutations in the cancer cells. These mutations can give rise to proteins called neoantigens, which help to distinguish cancer cells from healthy ones.

Eric Fomley’s stories have appeared in Clarkesworld, Flash Fiction Online and Daily Science Fiction.

I’m in an Obelisk Corporation jump ship, strapped into a drop pod. The harness is tight across my chest and the metal walls rattle as we skirt across the atmosphere of some planet.

Command wants us to keep these logs. They say it will keep our minds sharp before each drop, and help us remember what we’re fighting for. The other soldiers don’t think the war will last long. I hope they’re right so I can get back home to you.

I’m nervous about the reprinting, though. I don’t like the idea of body switching, no matter how much they guarantee the transfers are perfect. But as nervous as facing the NC soldiers makes me, there is some comfort knowing that if I’m killed I’ll be reprinted. It takes a lot of the fear out of those pre-battle nerves. It’s also nice knowing I’ll come home to you in the same condition I left you.

As I’m sitting here waiting for the drop, I keep thinking about our last moments together on the tarmac. The way you smelled when we hugged. The way you kissed me like you didn’t want to let go.

Space is a cold place, but today that memory of you makes me warm.

I’m in an Obelisk jump ship, strapped into a drop pod. Same type as before. This ship shakes a little more than the last one.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

It’s gone on longer than anyone here thought it would. Fighting a war across this many planets and moons has dragged it out. What was supposed to be a quick operation has turned into a slugfest.

I’ve been reprinted a few times now and it isn’t as scary as I thought it would be. It’s hard to shake the final moments before my ‘deaths’, though. Those stay with me. I still remember the feeling of the plasma round that got me last time. The heat, the sudden quiet as I slipped into darkness. My last thoughts of you.

It’s still traumatic, even when I wake up in the printing bay fresh and uninjured. Sometimes at night I replay those moments in my mind whether I want to or not.

There’s a place we used to eat. I forget the name of it now, but that steakhouse in your hometown was always such a nice place to take you. It became ours. I loved those long hours we spent there talking over dinner while the place emptied around us.

I’m in the jump ship, strapped into a drop pod. I think it’s the same type as before. Hard to tell any more.

I have no idea how many times I’ve dropped now. This war feels like it will never end and I want to get out of here so bad. I’m tired of the killing. I’m tired of the dying.

Something is wrong with the transfers. I can’t quite pin down what it is. Our bodies seem perfect every time, but something is … off in the mind. Details that shouldn’t be fuzzy are starting to blur. A few of us raised concerns with our CO, but it didn’t go anywhere.

I was thinking about our wedding day earlier. I don’t know quite how to say this, but I’m having trouble remembering some of the smaller details. The colours we chose. The music the DJ played. I know it was beautiful, I remember that much.

I need to get out of this cycle. For the war to be over. I want to see you. So you can help me fill in some of the gaps I feel.

I’m in the jump ship, strapped into a pod.

One of my closest friends reprinted yesterday and he acted like he didn’t know me. I told him about the time we got drunk after that drop on Rebulyan II. He just stared at me with empty eyes. Like I was a stranger.

So much of my mind feels like it hasn’t transferred. Silly things I should know are slipping away. Words get stuck sometimes. Names, too. We’ve been asked not to bring it up to our COs anymore. Which tells me they know it’s a problem.

I tried to remember your face today. The way you look at me, your eyes, your hair and the way you smile. I feel you slipping away from me and I don’t want to lose you.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03108-w

Theranos, the failed blood-testing company founded by Elizabeth Holmes, claimed that its device could run hundreds of tests on a few drops of blood.Credit: HBO Documentary Films/Everett Collection

You Can See Everything chronicles the final weeks before disgraced entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes went to prison in 2023. Since its US release last week, the film has thrust Holmes and her failed blood-testing start-up, Theranos, back into the spotlight. For the biotechnology industry, however, the spectre of Theranos never went away.

Blood, sweat and tears in biotech — the Theranos story

Blood, sweat and tears in biotech — the Theranos story

More than a decade after the company’s spectacular collapse, a new generation of diagnostics firms still grapples with the fallout. During the 2010s, Theranos said that its device could run hundreds of tests on only a few drops of blood, drastically reducing the amount of fluid needed for routine diagnostics. The company’s success soared as investors backed the technology, but US federal juries later ruled that Theranos had misled those financial supporters about its device’s capabilities, and two of its executives, including Holmes, were sentenced to more than a decade in prison.

Today, health-tech companies are still developing devices similar to the ones that Theranos aspired to make. The firms say that Theranos’s demise underscored the importance of transparency in their pursuit. “Trust in diagnostics has to be earned through evidence and not promises,” says Dena Marrinucci, co-founder of Truvian Health, a diagnostics company in San Diego, California.

Theranos left “a crater in the whole field of monitoring and diagnostics”, says Paul Yager, a bioengineer and diagnostics developer at the University of Washington in Seattle. For years after its collapse, he says, researchers pitching blood-testing technologies faced the same opening question in every meeting: “How is what you’re trying to do different from what Theranos did?”

Standard diagnostic tests, which can measure everything from the levels of basic minerals — or electrolytes — to hormones in the blood, typically require several vials of fluid drawn from a person’s arm to ensure a large, homogeneous sample. The results can be used to diagnose and track various health conditions.

Theranos, which was based in Palo Alto, California, claimed that its Edison device could execute hundreds of diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood from a finger prick. But behind the scenes, the company was having a hard time making the platform work as advertised, and instead resorted to diluting patient samples and running them on standard blood-testing machines from other companies, in some cases producing skewed measurements.

In You Can See Everything, filmmaker Nathan Fielder (left) captured Elizabeth Holmes’s final days with her family before she went to prison for defrauding investors.Credit: A24/Everett Collection

Although many factors probably contributed to Theranos’s failures, says Eric Olson, founder of Babson Diagnostics in Austin, Texas, one of them was using blood from a finger prick rather than an arm vein. This introduces the potential for contamination of the sample. For example, sometimes squeezing the fingertip to extract blood droplets can cause blood cells to burst as they emerge from the skin, leaking debris into samples and causing erroneous measurements.

Tiny blood volumes also run into a statistics problem, Yager says. Measuring an abundant molecule in the blood, such as glucose, requires only a small droplet because a person’s bloodstream is chock-full of the sugar. But many other molecules that are biomarkers of disease, such as viral particles from an HIV infection, circulate at much lower concentrations. In a few microlitres of blood from a finger prick, those molecules might barely register on a device’s detector.

Despite those challenges, the biotechnology industry hasn’t given up on Theranos’s goal. That is because making rapid blood monitoring more accessible remains an urgent problem, Yager says, especially for people who live in rural areas that are far from centralized laboratories, and for older and disabled people who struggle to travel to medical appointments.

How blowing the whistle on the Theranos scandal transformed Erika Cheung’s career

How blowing the whistle on the Theranos scandal transformed Erika Cheung’s career

Over the past year in particular, Yager says, the number of blood-testing start-ups has multiplied so quickly that he has struggled to keep track of them. He thinks that the commercial boom is being driven in large part by ultra-rich people and social-media influencers who are urging seemingly-healthy consumers to pay for biomarker tests, many of which have not yet been validated, in a bid to extend their lifespan.

Rather than trying to defy the limitations that Theranos struggled with, some companies are attempting to engineer their way around them. Olson says that BetterWay, the blood-testing service at Babson Diagnostics, has standardized the typical finger-prick collection method with a specialized device that extracts 6–12 drops of blood and reduces the likelihood of cell damage.

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

An outbreak of Shamonda virus was detected in cows in Europe in July and is ongoing.Credit: Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty

An individual with cancer in France has become the first person known to contract the Shamonda virus, after an outbreak in livestock in Europe that was first identified in July. The man, aged in his sixties, died on 9 October, 16 days after he started showing neurological symptoms, including vision loss and confusion, according to a case report published in Eurosurveillance this week1. Infectious-disease researchers say little is known about the virus or how it affects the body.

The man lived in a rural area in the Rhône–Alpes region, where Shamonda virus has been detected in cattle. He was probably infected after being bitten by midges, the report states.

It is also possible that he contracted the virus by eating contaminated food or through a blood transfusion or transplant, although the report’s authors say these routes are less likely. “Investigations are ongoing to rule them out,” they write. Researchers say that the risk of the virus being transmitted between people is low.

Shamonda virus belongs to a family of viruses called orthobunyaviruses, which are known to infect animals such as cows and deer, and are transmitted by mosquitoes and midges, says Krispin Hajkowicz, an infectious-disease researcher at the University of Queensland, Australia. There are no vaccines or antiviral treatments for orthobunyaviruses, Hajkowicz says.

More orthobunyaviruses are being detected in people, says Daniel Rawle, a virologist at the QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute in Brisbane, Australia. Climate change and greater contact between wildlife, livestock and humans are some of the factors that have increased the risk of people becoming infected. Another element is that a growing number of people are immunocompromised, and so more at risk of being infected and developing life-threatening symptoms. Although no human-to-human transmission has been recorded for these viruses, during an outbreak of an orthobunyavirus called Oropouche in Brazil in 2024, transmission was reported between pregnant women and their fetuses.

The individual in France, who had leukaemia and was severely immunocompromised, started having seizures shortly after the onset of symptoms and went into a coma, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. When his symptoms did not improve after treatment with antibiotics, an antiviral drug and high doses of corticosteroids, he was taken off life support.

Andrew Robinson is a writer based in London and author of Earthshock (1993), The Story of Measurement (2007) and Einstein in Oxford (2024).

Danni Holmes Melbourne Univ. Press (2026)

“If a fully-fledged quantum computer arrived on our doorstep today, it would be like giving a caveman a smartphone,” writes physicist Danni Holmes. Her first book is a sparkling analysis of the quantum world. It takes the non-physicist reader through the laws of classical physics discovered by Isaac Newton and James Clerk Maxwell to more-recent fascinating facets of the field, such as the reason why black holes don’t last forever and whether human consciousness could have a quantum origin.

Any study of the US pharmaceutical industry involves finance as well as science, as journalist Barry Werth unpacked in his first book, The Billion-Dollar Molecule. His latest book discusses the United States’ “eighty-year-long preeminence in drug research”, which began during the Second World War under the direction of presidential science adviser Vannevar Bush. Focusing on Bush and five post-war leaders in the field of pharmacology, such as Max Tishler, Werth illuminates the value of long-term investment in science.

Communication researcher Xiaochang Li describes her complex book as a cultural history of both technology and communication. It analyses “how words became data, how data became imperative, and how the problem of language came to shape the very foundations of algorithmic culture” — including for large language models and artificial intelligence. Li recounts vigorous debates between linguists, computer scientists and communication engineers, triggered by the thorny relationship between speech and writing.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain at high risk of relapse despite perioperative treatment1-3. NeoCOAST-2 (NCT05061550), a phase 2, randomised platform trial, tested novel perioperative treatments in patients with stage IIA–IIIB NSCLC. At primary analysis, combining standard chemotherapy plus durvalumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) with oleclumab (Arm 1, n = 76), monalizumab (Arm 2, n = 72) or datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd; Arm 4, n = 54) resulted in pathological complete response (pCR) rates of 20.3%, 25.7%, and 35.2%, respectively4. Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes. The 24-month EFS rates were 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% in Arms 1, 2 and 4, respectively. Using a tumour-agnostic assay, ctDNA clearance at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 Day 1 was highest in Arm 4 (50.9%, 54.5%, and 72.5% in each arm, respectively). ctDNA clearance correlated with prolonged EFS versus non-clearance (pooled hazard ratio (HR) 0.22; 95% CI = 0.11–0.45, P = 0.0000443). Patients with both ctDNA clearance and pCR had favourable EFS outcomes versus those with neither (EFS HR 0.10, 95% CI = 0.02–0.42, P = 0.002). These findings suggest combined assessment of ctDNA clearance and pCR may improve risk stratification, and that the numerically highest pCR4 and EFS rates with the Dato-DXd combination warrant further evaluation.

Why pipes sometimes get "stuck": buffering

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Here’s a niche terminal problem that has bothered me for years but that I never really understood until a few weeks ago. Let’s say you’re running this command to watch for some specific output in a log file:

If log lines are being added to the file relatively slowly, the result I’d see is… nothing! It doesn’t matter if there were matches in the log file or not, there just wouldn’t be any output.

I internalized this as “uh, I guess pipes just get stuck sometimes and don’t show me the output, that’s weird”, and I’d handle it by just running grep thing1 /some/log/file | grep thing2 instead, which would work.

So as I’ve been doing a terminal deep dive over the last few months I was really excited to finally learn exactly why this happens.

The reason why “pipes get stuck” sometimes is that it’s VERY common for programs to buffer their output before writing it to a pipe or file. So the pipe is working fine, the problem is that the program never even wrote the data to the pipe!

This is for performance reasons: writing all output immediately as soon as you can uses more system calls, so it’s more efficient to save up data until you have 8KB or so of data to write (or until the program exits) and THEN write it to the pipe.

the problem is that grep thing1 is saving up all of its matches until it has 8KB of data to write, which might literally never happen.

Part of why I found this so disorienting is that tail -f file | grep thing will work totally fine, but then when you add the second grep, it stops working!! The reason for this is that the way grep handles buffering depends on whether it’s writing to a terminal or not.

Here’s how grep (and many other programs) decides to buffer its output:

So if grep is writing directly to your terminal then you’ll see the line as soon as it’s printed, but if it’s writing to a pipe, you won’t.

Of course the buffer size isn’t always 8KB for every program, it depends on the implementation. For grep the buffering is handled by libc, and libc’s buffer size is defined in the BUFSIZ variable. Here’s where that’s defined in glibc.

(as an aside: “programs do not use 8KB output buffers when writing to a terminal” isn’t, like, a law of terminal physics, a program COULD use an 8KB buffer when writing output to a terminal if it wanted, it would just be extremely weird if it did that, I can’t think of any program that behaves that way)

One annoying thing about this buffering behaviour is that you kind of need to remember which commands buffer their output when writing to a pipe.

Some commands that don’t buffer their output:

I think almost everything else will buffer output, especially if it’s a command where you’re likely to be using it for batch processing. Here’s a list of some common commands that buffer their output when writing to a pipe, along with the flag that disables block buffering.

Those are all the ones I can think of, lots of unix commands (like sort) may or may not buffer their output but it doesn’t matter because sort can’t do anything until it finishes receiving input anyway.

Also I did my best to test both the Mac OS and GNU versions of these but there are a lot of variations and I might have made some mistakes.

Also, here are a few programming language where the default print statement will buffer output when writing to a pipe, and some ways to disable buffering if you want:

I assume that these languages are designed this way so that the default print function will be fast when you’re doing batch processing.

Also whether output is buffered or not might depend on how you print, for example in C++ cout << "hello\n" buffers when writing to a pipe but cout << "hello" << endl will flush its output.

Let’s say you’re running this command as a hacky way to watch for DNS requests to example.com, and you forgot to pass -l to tcpdump:

When you press Ctrl-C, what happens? In a magical perfect world, what I would want to happen is for tcpdump to flush its buffer, grep would search for example.com, and I would see all the output I missed.

But in the real world, what happens is that all the programs get killed and the output in tcpdump’s buffer is lost.

I think this problem is probably unavoidable – I spent a little time with strace to see how this works and grep receives the SIGINT before tcpdump anyway so even if tcpdump tried to flush its buffer grep would already be dead.

After a little more investigation, there is a workaround: if you find tcpdump’s PID and kill -TERM $PID, then tcpdump will flush the buffer so you can see the output. That’s kind of a pain but I tested it and it seems to work.

It’s not just pipes, this will also buffer:

Redirecting to a file doesn’t have the same “Ctrl-C will totally destroy the contents of the buffer” problem though – in my experience it usually behaves more like you’d want, where the contents of the buffer get written to the file before the program exits. I’m not 100% sure whether this is something you can always rely on or not.

Okay, let’s talk solutions. Let’s say you’ve run this command:

I asked people on Mastodon how they would solve this in practice and there were 5 basic approaches. Here they are:

Historically my solution to this has been to just avoid the “command writing to pipe slowly” situation completely and instead run a program that will finish quickly like this:

This doesn’t do the same thing as the original command but it does mean that you get to avoid thinking about these weird buffering issues.

(you could also do grep thing1 /some/log/file but I often prefer to use an “unnecessary” cat)

You could remember that grep has a flag to avoid buffering and pass it like this:

Some people said that if they’re specifically dealing with a multiple greps situation, they’ll rewrite it to use a single awk instead, like this:

Or you would write a more complicated grep, like this:

(awk also buffers, so for this to work you’ll want awk to be the last command in the pipeline)

stdbuf uses LD_PRELOAD to turn off libc’s buffering, and you can use it to turn off output buffering like this:

Like any LD_PRELOAD solution it’s a bit unreliable – it doesn’t work on static binaries, I think won’t work if the program isn’t using libc’s buffering, and doesn’t always work on Mac OS. Harry Marr has a really nice How stdbuf works post.

unbuffer program will force the program’s output to be a TTY, which means that it’ll behave the way it normally would on a TTY (less buffering, colour output, etc). You could use it in this example like this:

Unlike stdbuf it will always work, though it might have unwanted side effects, for example grep thing1’s will also colour matches.

If you want to install unbuffer, it’s in the expect package.

It’s a bit hard for me to say which one is “best”, I think personally I’m mostly likely to use unbuffer because I know it’s always going to work.

If I learn about more solutions I’ll try to add them to this post.

I think it’s not very common for me to have a program that slowly trickles data into a pipe like this, normally if I’m using a pipe a bunch of data gets written very quickly, processed by everything in the pipeline, and then everything exits. The only examples I can come up with right now are:

I think it would be cool if there were a standard environment variable to turn off buffering, like PYTHONUNBUFFERED in Python. I got this idea from a couple of blog posts by Mark Dominus in 2018. Maybe NO_BUFFER like NO_COLOR?

The design seems tricky to get right; Mark points out that NETBSD has environment variables called STDBUF, STDBUF1, etc which gives you a ton of control over buffering but I imagine most developers don’t want to implement many different environment variables to handle a relatively minor edge case.

I’m also curious about whether there are any programs that just automatically flush their output buffers after some period of time (like 1 second). It feels like it would be nice in theory but I can’t think of any program that does that so I imagine there are some downsides.

Some things I didn’t talk about in this post since these posts have been getting pretty long recently and seriously does anyone REALLY want to read 3000 words about buffering?
